title: Conflicting advice on whether it's safe to discharge a capacitor with a screwdriver
summary: Forum wisdom says short it with a screwdriver; textbook caution says never. Both are talking about different capacitors. Here is how to sort it out.

blocks.title: Two confident answers, one missing question
blocks.body: Ask whether you can discharge a capacitor with a screwdriver and the internet splits in half: 'everyone does it' versus 'never do it.' The fight exists because both sides are answering about different capacitors without saying so. The missing question is always: which capacitor, charged to what, holding how much energy?

columns.name: Camp: just short it
columns.detail: Comes from tube-radio and CRT repair culture, where caps hold hundreds of volts at modest energy and the screwdriver is always in your hand. Their method 'works': bang, spark, discharged - with pitting on the screwdriver and stress on the capacitor as uncounted costs.

columns.name: Camp: never short it
columns.detail: Comes from electronics teaching and from people who have seen a low-ESR bank dump hundreds of amps through a dead short - welded screwdrivers, exploded cans, damaged dielectrics. Their rule survives every case, but treats a 10 uF signal cap and a photoflash bank as the same animal.

columns.name: The synthesis
columns.detail: Discharge through a resistor, sized to the capacitor. The resistor turns a violent event into a boring one. Boring is the goal.

blocks.heading: What you are actually dealing with
rows: Signal / coupling cap, 10 uF at 25 V
Harmless but pointless - a resistor or even a meter lead does it without drama
SMPS bulk cap, 470 uF at 400 V
Shorting pits tools and can crack the cap's internals. Resistor, always
Microwave oven cap, 1 uF at 2,100 V
Never a screwdriver - the voltage outlives bad technique. Resistor with insulated leads, then verify
A dead short here is an arc-flash experiment. Bleeder resistor and a procedure
Shorting makes a heater and a welder, not a shock. Resistor to protect the cell
blocks.caption: Energy is 1/2 x C x V^2. The voltage term is squared, which is why high-voltage small caps deserve more respect than big-voltage numbers suggest and low-voltage big caps get disrespected wrongly.

blocks.heading: The boring, correct method
items: Identify the capacitor and estimate its voltage rating - assume it is charged to that.
Pick a resistor that limits current to something tame: for hundreds of volts, a few kilohms at a suitable wattage is the classic choice.
Connect the resistor across the terminals with insulated leads or clips. Never your fingers.
Wait: five time constants (5 x R x C) brings it under 1% of the starting voltage.
Verify with a meter before touching anything. The meter reading near zero is the discharge, not the elapsed time.
Treat anything that cannot be verified as still charged.

blocks.heading: Why the advice stays conflicting
blocks.body: Each camp generalizes from its own bench. The radio restorer's 450 V electrolytic tolerates decades of screwdriver shorts, so the habit feels proven. The power engineer's motor-drive bank turns the same habit into an explosion, so the prohibition feels absolute. Advice conflicts most where experience is narrowest - and capacitor energy spans six orders of magnitude, so 'a capacitor' is nearly a contentless word. When advice conflicts, find the variable the advisors disagree on silently. Here it is energy and ESR. Ask 'charged to what, holding how much' and the conflict dissolves.

blocks.title: The cautious reader's takeaway
blocks.body: If you cannot identify the capacitor, its voltage, or its energy, you do not yet know whether it is safe to touch at all - discharged is a measurement, not an assumption. A resistor, insulated leads, and a verifying meter cover every case on this page. The screwdriver covers none of them well.
